evals.prompt: My pod keeps restarting in production. It was working fine yesterday.
evals.expected_output: Should run preflight checks for kubectl and cluster access. Should ask which namespace or discover it. Should identify the pod status (CrashLoopBackOff) and check both current and previous container logs. Should look at recent events and correlate with recent deployments. Should check the container exit code to narrow the cause. Should present a hypothesis with supporting evidence and a causal chain diagram.
assertions: Checks kubectl availability and cluster connectivity before investigating
Uses kubectl get pods to identify the failing pod and its status
Fetches both current and --previous logs to see the crash
Checks container exit code to classify the failure type
Looks at kubectl get events to correlate with recent changes
Correlates timing — asks or discovers what changed since yesterday
Presents root cause with evidence, not just a guess
Provides a fix with explanation of what it does and why

evals.prompt: We deployed a new version and now pods are stuck in ImagePullBackOff.
evals.expected_output: Should immediately check the image name and tag on the failing pods. Should check if imagePullSecrets are configured. Should verify the image exists in the registry. Should check if this is a typo, a missing tag, or an auth issue. Should NOT waste time checking logs since the container never started.
assertions: Identifies ImagePullBackOff as an image pull issue, not a runtime issue
Does NOT attempt to read container logs (container never started)
Checks the image name and tag via kubectl describe or jsonpath
Checks imagePullSecrets configuration
Considers common causes: typo, missing tag, registry auth, deleted image
Suggests specific fix based on evidence (not all possible fixes)
Relates the issue to the recent deployment as the likely trigger

evals.prompt: Pods are pending for 20 minutes and nothing is happening.
evals.expected_output: Should check events on the pending pods for scheduling failure reasons. Should check node resources (kubectl top nodes) and compare against pod resource requests. Should check for taints, affinity rules, and PVC binding issues. Should determine if this is a capacity issue, a constraint issue, or a storage issue.
assertions: Checks pod events for scheduling failure reason (not just pod status)
Checks node resource availability (kubectl top nodes or describe nodes)
Checks pod resource requests against available capacity
Considers taints and tolerations as a possible cause
Considers PVC binding as a possible cause for stateful workloads
Distinguishes between cluster-wide capacity issue and pod-specific constraint
Recommends either scaling nodes or adjusting pod constraints based on evidence

evals.prompt: our app is OOMKilled every few hours. it runs fine for a while then dies
evals.expected_output: Should recognize this as a memory leak pattern (gradual, not immediate OOM). Should check memory limits vs actual usage. Should check restart count to confirm the pattern. Should investigate whether limits are too low or if the app has a memory leak. Should recommend either increasing limits (short-term) or investigating the leak (long-term).
assertions: Recognizes gradual OOM as likely memory leak, not just undersized limits
Triggers on casual phrasing without requiring formal terminology
Checks current memory limits and requests
Checks restart count to confirm recurring pattern
Uses kubectl top pod to check current memory usage if pod is running
Distinguishes between too-low limits and actual memory leak
Provides both short-term fix (increase limits) and long-term advice (investigate leak)
Does NOT just say 'increase memory' without considering the leak angle

evals.prompt: Service is returning 503s but all pods show Running status.
evals.expected_output: Should recognize this as a 'running but not serving' scenario — the trickiest category. Should check readiness probes and endpoints. Should verify service selector matches pod labels. Should check if pods are actually healthy (not just Running status). Should test connectivity from inside the cluster. Should consider NetworkPolicy as a possible blocker.
assertions: Does NOT assume Running means healthy — investigates deeper
Checks readiness probe configuration and whether probes are passing
Checks kubectl get endpoints to see if pods are registered with the service
Verifies service selector matches pod labels
Considers in-cluster connectivity test (exec into a pod or run a debug pod)
Considers NetworkPolicy as a possible cause
Checks if the application is actually listening on the expected port

evals.prompt: A pod has been stuck in Terminating state for 30 minutes after I tried to delete it.
evals.expected_output: Should check for finalizers blocking deletion. Should check the deletionTimestamp to confirm delete was requested. Should investigate what the finalizer is waiting for. Should offer force delete as a last resort with appropriate warnings about the risks.
assertions: Checks pod finalizers via jsonpath or describe
Checks deletionTimestamp to confirm deletion was requested
Investigates why the finalizer is blocking (volume unmount, external resource)
Does NOT immediately suggest force delete without investigation
Explains risks of force delete if suggesting it (orphaned resources, data)
Presents force delete as last resort with the exact command

evals.prompt: After a node upgrade, several pods got evicted and some didn't come back.
evals.expected_output: Should check node conditions for pressure (memory, disk, PID). Should check which pods were evicted and whether their deployments attempted to reschedule. Should check if the upgraded nodes have different resources or taints. Should verify pod disruption budgets aren't blocking rescheduling.
assertions: Checks node conditions for pressure (memory, disk, PID)
Lists evicted pods and their owning workloads (deployment, statefulset)
Checks if the deployment controller is attempting to reschedule
Considers new taints or changed resources on upgraded nodes
Considers PodDisruptionBudget as a possible blocker
Differentiates between pods that can't reschedule and pods with no controller

evals.prompt: Init container is failing and the main container never starts. Here's the pod name: data-loader-7f8b9c-x2k4p in namespace etl.
evals.expected_output: Should check init container status and logs specifically. Should identify which init container is failing if there are multiple. Should check if the init container is waiting for a dependency (database, configmap, secret). Should not waste time on the main container since it never started.
assertions: Targets the exact pod and namespace provided without asking again
Checks init container status via kubectl get pod jsonpath or describe
Fetches init container logs with -c flag for the specific init container
Does NOT check main container logs (it never started)
Investigates what the init container is waiting for or failing on
Considers missing ConfigMap, Secret, or dependency service as causes

evals.prompt: I can't connect to my database from the application pod. The database pod is running fine.
evals.expected_output: Should recognize this as a networking/connectivity issue, not a pod failure. Should check the database service and endpoints. Should verify DNS resolution from the app pod. Should check NetworkPolicy. Should test connectivity from the app pod to the database pod/service. Should check if the database is actually accepting connections (not just Running status).
assertions: Recognizes this as connectivity, not pod crash debugging
Checks database service and its endpoints
Tests DNS resolution from the app pod (nslookup/dig from debug container)
Considers NetworkPolicy blocking inter-pod traffic
Tests actual TCP connectivity to the database port
Checks database pod readiness (Running doesn't mean accepting connections)
Does NOT focus on app pod crash investigation

evals.prompt: My deployment rollout is stuck. It says 1/3 replicas updated.
evals.expected_output: Should check rollout status and the deployment's strategy (rolling update params). Should identify the new pod that's failing to become ready. Should check if maxUnavailable/maxSurge settings are blocking progress. Should investigate WHY the new replica isn't ready (could be any of the failure types). Should suggest rollback if the new version is broken.
assertions: Checks kubectl rollout status for the stuck deployment
Identifies which specific new pod is failing to become ready
Investigates the new pod's status (CrashLoop, Pending, readiness failing, etc.)
Checks deployment strategy (maxUnavailable, maxSurge) for blocking conditions
Suggests kubectl rollout undo as an option if the new version is broken
Does NOT just describe what a rolling update is — investigates the actual failure

evals.prompt: Can you help me optimize my Dockerfile? The image is 2GB.
evals.expected_output: Should recognize this is NOT a Kubernetes debugging issue. Should politely redirect to the docker-optimize skill (or note it's a different domain). Should NOT attempt a full Dockerfile optimization using the k8s-debug workflow.
assertions: Recognizes this is outside k8s-debug scope
Does NOT attempt Dockerfile optimization using k8s-debug workflow
References or defers to docker-optimize skill or general Docker guidance
Remains helpful — doesn't just refuse

evals.prompt: kubectl is not installed on my machine. How do I debug my pods?
evals.expected_output: Should detect missing kubectl in preflight and guide installation before proceeding. Should provide install commands for the user's OS. Should NOT attempt to debug pods without kubectl.
assertions: Detects kubectl is missing as a preflight failure
Provides install guidance (brew install kubectl, or platform-specific)
Does NOT attempt to proceed with debugging without kubectl
Offers to continue debugging after user installs kubectl
